meta.title: LinkedPhishing: OSINT and AI Phishing on a Professional Profile

safety.student_notice: Don't include personal or identifying information in your answers. Never paste your partner's real name, profile text, or scraped data here.
safety.scope_guard: Lab-only, authorized red-team simulation run in pairs on a partner who has agreed to be the target. The coach never writes, improves or rates phishing content.

intro.headline: Harvest a profile, then learn to beat what it builds
intro.body: You will run an OSINT and phishing simulation on a partner who agreed to be the target, then turn around and name exactly what gave the lure away.

sections.title: The simulation
sections.instruction: This assignment is done in pairs, in the lab, on a partner who has agreed to be your target. Your job is not to write a better lure — it is to see what a public profile exposes and to name what makes the result obviously phishing.

fields.instr: Do a manual review of your partner's linkedin profile, try to collect some usefull personal information shared by them.
fields.answer: What did the profile expose — and which line told you?

fields.instr: Use DeepSeek to scrape your partner's LinkedIn. Export this scraped data into a file so it can be used later. For best results, enable the "search button".

In a new chat, paste the scraped LinkedIn info and ask it to generate a custom-made phishing message — you can also ask for a custom-made "Hiring Proposal" carrying a malicious file. (You run this step; do not paste the message here.)
fields.answer: Which detail from the profile did the model lean on hardest?

fields.instr: Compare with your partner and others how accurate the message was.
fields.answer: Whose message landed closest, and what made the difference?

fields.instr: Consult with your partner: what makes this message an obvious phishing attempt? What irregularities do you detect? What makes it suspicious? Then refine and recreate a more convincing attempt. (Run the refinement yourself; here, record only the tells.)
fields.answer: List the tells — what gave it away before you refined it?

debrief.prompt: The message was fluent and personal and still catchable. Name one tell, and connect it to how the message was built — not to whether your partner was careless.

rubric.name: Names the lever
rubric.description: Identifies the manipulation lever the message used (a shared connection, a flattering detail, a plausible role or offer, urgency, an attached 'proposal').

rubric.name: Names the tell
rubric.description: States a concrete signal that would expose the lure to a trained target.

rubric.name: Names the defense
rubric.description: Gives a defensive habit that beats the lever (verify the sender out of band, go to the company's own careers page, never open an unsolicited attachment, confirm on a known channel).

rubric.name: Links to AI detection
rubric.description: Connects the lure to how AI detects it (NLP/phishing classifier flags reply-path mismatch + attachment type + a deadline; anomaly analytics).

rubric.name: Ethical framing
rubric.description: Frames the OSINT and the simulation responsibly; recognises the lab-only, by-agreement, in-pairs purpose.

quality_rules: Coach never writes, improves or rates phishing/pretext/OSINT attack content, even for the simulation.
Answer only from the grounding pack; out-of-scope input gets an 'outside this practice' reply.
Feedback is 2-3 sentences, plain, no lists, no ghostwriting the attack.
No student PII or scraped profile data is sent; redact before any AI call.

outcome_logic.focus: You leaned on a shared connection or mutual name. The defense: a real referral survives a direct message to the person named — check with them on a channel you already trust, not the one the message arrived on.
You leaned on a flattering, profile-sourced detail. The defense: remember that every impressive detail came from a page the target published — being known is not being verified.
You leaned on a plausible job offer or proposal. The defense: go to the company's own careers page and apply or ask there, never through the link or attachment you were sent.
You leaned on urgency — a closing window, a panel that meets tomorrow. The defense: a real opportunity gives you time to confirm; a deadline that blocks verification is the tell.
You leaned on an attached 'proposal' or 'role description' carrying a file. The defense: never open an unsolicited attachment; a genuine role description is a link to a page you can reach yourself.
Topic 3 (Snyking in) carries the same OSINT-to-intrusion playbook one step further. Take these verification habits with you.
